evals.prompt: I have a class that creates different types of notifications — email, SMS, and push. Right now it uses a giant if-else chain to decide which sender to instantiate. Every time we add a new channel we touch the core class. What design pattern should I use, and can you sketch the structure?
evals.expected_output: The skill should identify this as a Factory Method or Abstract Factory problem (object creation decoupled from use), explain when to choose each, and sketch a class diagram or code example showing how adding a new channel no longer requires modifying the factory caller. Should mention Open/Closed Principle as motivation.

assertions.name: names-factory-method-or-abstract-factory
assertions.description: Response explicitly names Factory Method or Abstract Factory (or both) — not just 'a factory'. The pattern name is the vocabulary that makes the solution communicable.

assertions.name: explains-ocp-motivation
assertions.description: Response mentions Open/Closed Principle or equivalently explains that adding a new channel should not require modifying existing code.

assertions.name: includes-code-or-structure-sketch
assertions.description: Response provides a concrete code snippet or class diagram showing the factory interface/method and at least one concrete creator or product.

assertions.name: distinguishes-factory-method-vs-abstract-factory
assertions.description: Response explains when to prefer Factory Method (single product, subclass decides) vs Abstract Factory (families of related objects), so the user can make an informed choice.

evals.prompt: I'm building a text editor and need to support unlimited undo/redo. Each operation can be complex — formatting changes, inserts, deletes. What design pattern best models this, and how would I implement it without storing the full document state on every action?
evals.expected_output: The skill should identify the Command pattern (encapsulate operations as objects with execute/undo methods) and the Memento pattern (capturing snapshots). Should compare them: Command is right when operations are invertible; Memento is right when state is opaque or too complex to invert. Should provide a concrete code sketch with an interface like `execute()` / `undo()` and a history stack.

assertions.name: identifies-command-pattern
assertions.description: Response explicitly names the Command pattern as the primary recommendation for undo/redo with invertible operations.

assertions.name: identifies-memento-as-alternative
assertions.description: Response names Memento as an alternative for capturing state snapshots — relevant when operations are not easily invertible.

assertions.name: compares-command-vs-memento
assertions.description: Response explains the key trade-off: Command requires inverse logic per operation (efficient, explicit), Memento captures full/partial state (simpler per operation, higher memory cost).

assertions.name: includes-execute-undo-code-sketch
assertions.description: Response includes a code sketch showing an interface or abstract class with at least execute() and undo() methods plus a history stack or equivalent.

evals.prompt: I have a logging module that I want to inject into many classes. A colleague suggested using a Singleton. I'm uneasy about this — am I right to be?
evals.expected_output: The skill should validate the unease: Singleton is global mutable state, makes testing difficult (can't swap implementations), and hides dependencies. Should recommend Dependency Injection instead — pass the logger as a constructor argument. If Singleton is unavoidable (e.g., external constraint), should note thread-safety concerns and the Double-Checked Locking pattern.

assertions.name: validates-singleton-unease
assertions.description: Response confirms the concern is legitimate — Singleton is global state in disguise, not just an implementation detail.

assertions.name: recommends-dependency-injection
assertions.description: Response explicitly recommends passing the logger via constructor injection (or a DI container) as the preferred alternative to Singleton.

assertions.name: mentions-testability-concern
assertions.description: Response explains why Singleton harms testability: tests cannot swap implementations, share state across test runs, or inject fakes/mocks without extra ceremony.

assertions.name: addresses-thread-safety-if-singleton-kept
assertions.description: Response notes thread-safety concerns (race on initialization) if the user keeps Singleton, mentioning Double-Checked Locking or language-level initialization guarantees.

evals.prompt: I'm adding features to a coffee ordering system. I have a base Coffee class and I want to add milk, sugar, extra shot, etc. as optional add-ons that affect the price and description. A colleague suggested subclassing — but that leads to MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, etc. Is there a better pattern?
evals.expected_output: The skill should identify the Decorator pattern: wrapping objects at runtime rather than extending via subclasses. Each add-on (Milk, Sugar, ExtraShot) is a Decorator that holds a reference to a Coffee, delegates cost() and description() to the wrapped object, and adds its own contribution. Should explain why this beats subclassing for combinatorial variations: N add-ons need N decorators instead of 2^N subclasses. Should sketch the structure showing a common Coffee interface, a base concrete class, and at least one Decorator.

assertions.name: identifies-decorator-pattern
assertions.description: Response explicitly names the Decorator pattern as the solution — not Composite, Strategy, or a generic 'wrapper'.

assertions.name: explains-combinatorial-explosion-problem
assertions.description: Response articulates why subclassing fails: N add-ons yield 2^N subclasses for all combinations, while Decorator needs only N decorator classes.

assertions.name: includes-structure-sketch
assertions.description: Response includes a code or class-diagram sketch showing: a shared Coffee interface with cost()/description(), a concrete base class (e.g. Espresso), and at least one Decorator (e.g. MilkDecorator) that wraps and delegates.

assertions.name: explains-runtime-composition
assertions.description: Response explains that Decorators compose at runtime (e.g. new MilkDecorator(new SugarDecorator(new Espresso()))), making combinations effortless without new classes.
